AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Pneumatosis intestinalis (PI) is an uncommon and poorly understood condition. Although it can be an incidental finding in asymptomatic individuals, it can also be secondary to life-threatening bowel ischaemia and sepsis. In premature infants, it is a pathognomonic sign of necrotising enterocolitis. There is no consensus regarding management and long-term outcome of children with PI.

AbstractText.Label: AIM
AbstractText.content: Review of our experience of PI in children beyond the early infantile period.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Retrospective review of patient's records and radiological images from 2013 to 2015.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Eighteen patients (three girls) had radiologically confirmed PI. The median age was 4.5 years (range 8 months-13 years). Background medical conditions (number): short bowel syndrome (one), congenital heart disease (two), sickle cell disease (one), epilepsy (three), cerebral palsy (six), myotonic dystrophy (four) and peroxisomal biogenesis defect (one).Six children (33%) presented with abdominal distension, four (22%) with abdominal pain, three (17%) with bilious vomiting, two (11%) with diarrhoea and one (6%) with rectal bleeding. Two (11%) were asymptomatic. One had air in portal vein and two had pneumoperitoneum.All patients with symptomatic PI were treated conservatively with successful outcome and complete resolution of PI. None required surgical intervention.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: PI in children who are not on chemotherapy or immunosuppressant appears to follow a benign course and is responsive to conservative management. In contrast to adults, portal venous gas and pneumoperitoneum do not predict the need for surgical intervention.
